chunks: And Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn from Muhammad ibn Sinan from Abu al-Jarud Ziyad ibn al-Mundhir who said:

Abu al-Ward asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) while I was with him about a man who said to his wife, 'You are upon me like the back of my mother' one hundred times. Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) said: 'He is able to free one slave for each time.' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then he is able to feed sixty poor people one hundred times.' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Then he is able to fast two consecutive months one hundred times.' He said: 'No.' He said: 'They are divided between him.'

key_terms.الظَّهْر: Zahar, a specific form of divorce where a husband compares his wife's back to his mother's back
key_terms.يُفَرَّقُ بَيْنَهُمَا: They are divided (referring to the expiations being shared or apportioned)

ai.seo_question: What is the expiation for saying 'Zahar' multiple times to one's wife according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Baqir clarifies that multiple instances of *Zihar* require cumulative expiation, offering a tiered scale of compensation based on the husband's financial capacity. The Imam concludes that if the cumulative burden becomes excessive, the expiations are divided among the available options rather than requiring the full sequence for each instance, reflecting the Shia principle of ease (*taysir*) in legal obligations. This ruling underscores the practical application of Quranic verses on *Zihar* within the context of family law and economic feasibility.
